desc:
List all n! orderings of 1..n in increasing lexicographic order and bend the list into a circle: the step after the last (fully descending) ordering leads back to the first (fully ascending) one.

You are given perm, one of these orderings, and a non-negative integer k. Walk k steps forward along the circle from perm and return the ordering where you land. A step is what the usual "next permutation" operation does.

perm = [1,2,3], k = 3   ->  [2,3,1]
perm = [3,2,1], k = 1   ->  [1,2,3]
perm = [2,1,3], k = 6   ->  [2,1,3]    (a full circle of 6 steps)
perm = [1,3,2], k = 10  ->  [3,2,1]
hints: Applying the next-permutation step k times is far too slow when k is in the billions. Is there a way to jump?
If you know the position (rank) of perm in the sorted list of all orderings, moving k steps just adds k to that rank, wrapping around after n! orderings.
Compute the rank with factorials (for each slot count the smaller numbers that come later), add k modulo n!, and turn the new rank back into an ordering by the factorial-base method.
editorial: Each ordering has a zero-based rank in the lexicographic list. For the rank, go through the slots: at slot i count how many numbers to the right of it are smaller than perm[i]; that count times (n-1-i)! summed over all slots is the rank.

Moving k steps (with wrap-around) gives the new rank (rank + k) mod n!. Convert it back by repeated division: for the slot with block size (n-1-i)! the quotient is the index into the sorted list of unused numbers, the remainder carries on. Both directions cost O(n2), and Python's big integers handle 20! without trouble; in languages with 64-bit integers 20! still fits.
Simulating the k steps is O(k · n), which only works for small k.
